name: edges of a broken concrete pavement area laid on dirt: the cracked concrete pads break into the dirt in small irregular chunks with a subtle darker lip under the break, with outer and inner corners, the full interior filled with the cracked concrete slab field
label: wasteland_ruins/slab-edge

surfaces.part: dirt ground field with cracked concrete pad patches (flat ground tiles viewed from above)

answer.evidence: This is a terrain autotile sheet (256x192 opaque, full width in every row), not a standing object. It shows a flat dirt field with irregular grey concrete pad patches and dark crack lines, seen from above. The column scans show repeating dirt and crack bands with no front-edge line, eave shadow or ellipse, and no vertical front face of 3 or more rows. The concrete patches have only a thin dark lip at the breaks, not a south face. It is a flat ground texture, so it reads as a top-down slab, which is expected for terrain.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate uses only 12 colours across two materials, so each ramp has about 4 steps: the dirt has 3-4 brown tones, and the concrete has light, mid, a darker crack tone and a few speckles. Beodeul uses 5-6 steps per material. Measured facts: 5 visible tones per tile, which is above the grass reference (3) but below the paving reference (7). Near-flat coverage is 1% and the dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so there is no flat-fill or black-outline problem. The weak point is the structure. The concrete chunks have no outline and no darker lip or shadow under the break, which the brief asks for. They read as pale shapes pasted on the dirt, with only a thin light rim. The scattered blobs and the single slab block on the right are thin on edge and corner variety. Texture is present (dirt grain, cracks, speckle) but shallower than the references. A careful artist would likely want more shading steps and a real break lip before accepting it beside the reference.

surfaces.part: cracked concrete pad fields on dirt (terrain tile sheet)

answer.evidence: The image is a terrain autotile sheet: grey cracked concrete patches on brown dirt, drawn flat from above. The silhouette is a full 256-wide block across rows 0-191, so there is no standing object. The concrete patches have irregular chunky edges and thin dark crack lines, and a few darker lips appear under some breaks. There is no front face, no eave line and no ellipse. Terrain tiles are meant to be flat ground, so a top-down read is expected for this kind.

styleAnswer.evidence: The whole candidate uses only 12 colours, about 5 visible tones per tile. That is below the paving reference's 7 and well short of Beodeul's 5-6 steps per material. The dirt has roughly 4 brown steps with speckle and blotches, so it reads as grainy rather than flat. The concrete chunks have only about 3-4 greys: a pale mid-grey body, a few darker crack lines and sparse light dots. Several chunks, especially the large slab at right, show broad pale areas with little per-chunk highlight or shadow. The 'darker lip under the break' is barely visible, so the chunks look pasted onto the dirt rather than shaded into it. There is no black sticker outline: dark edge pixels are 0% neutral and the cracks are tinted. But chunk edges are mostly abrupt value changes with no material-toned edge shading. Near-flat coverage is only 1%, so there are no flat fills. Overall it is a competent but shallower ramp than the reference, so it fails on shading depth and edge craft.

surfaces.part: cracked concrete pads and dirt ground, flat top-down terrain tile

answer.evidence: This is a flat terrain autotile sheet of concrete patches on dirt, seen from directly above. The silhouette is 256 wide on every row, so it is a full opaque tile field. The column scans show only alternating dirt and concrete texture bands with no front-edge line, no eave shadow, no ellipse and no vertical front face. The thin dark lines inside the concrete are cracks, not a south face. As a terrain tile it has no standing volume, so it reads as a flat top-down surface with no front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 5 visible tones per tile. That is above the grass reference (3) and a little below the paving reference (7). Near-flat coverage is 1%, so the dirt is mottled in several browns and the slabs carry speckle grain, with no large flat fills. Dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the crack and lip lines lean toward the material (darker blue-grey beside concrete, darker brown beside dirt), not a sticker-style black outline. Concrete chunks are separated mostly by value, which matches Beodeul practice. Weaknesses: each material ramp is only about 4 steps against Beodeul's 5-6, and the concrete has few highlight accents. The scattered chunks also read a bit sparse as edge pieces. Overall it is close enough to sit next to the references without looking sticker-like or flat.

surfaces.part: cracked concrete pads with irregular chunk edges, seen from above

answer.evidence: The whole 256x192 tile is a flat top-down view of grey concrete pads on brown dirt. The silhouette is a full 256-wide rectangle on every row. The column scans show only dirt texture runs (L about 81-115) and a few grey concrete runs, with no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no vertical face. The concrete pads have thin dark crack lines and ragged edges against the dirt, but no south-facing wall or lip of 3 or more rows. This is a plan-view ground texture, so there are no front-face rows.

styleAnswer.evidence: The whole candidate uses only 12 distinct colours across both materials. That gives about 4 steps for the grey concrete (light, mid, dark crack, a faint highlight) and 3-4 browns for the dirt, against roughly 6 steps in the Beodeul paving. It has 5 visible tones per tile against 7 for the paving reference. It is above the grass reference (3), but grass is a simpler material. Near-flat coverage is 1%, so the speckle and crack lines do break up the surfaces and there are no large flat fills. Dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the lips and crack lines are tinted and read as dark material tone, not sticker black. The concrete chunks are mostly one light grey with sparse crack strokes. They lack the per-stone shading and grain of the paving reference, and the dirt grain is a repetitive two-tone speckle with no clumps or pebbles. Overall it looks thinner and flatter than the Beodeul standard, so it fails.
